4593.prule: No positional word-stress rule is stated. Rawang (Mvtwang) is a register-tone language: three tones (high á, mid ā, low à) on tone-bearing syllables; every stop-final syllable (-p, -t, -ʔ, -k) is high-toned; open syllables written without a tone mark (the schwa-vowel prefix syllables, v = [ə]) are unstressed and toneless. Stress and tone-bearing coincide: a prefix syllable that fuses with the negative mv- 'will become stressed and so given a tone'.

4593.exq_: There are a number of morphophonemic processes which affect the segments and tones in connected speech. ... There are also often tone changes when certain suffixes, such as the reflexive/middle suffix -shì, is added to a verb.
4593.tone: LaPolla & Poa 2001:vii: three register tones on tone-bearing syllables (high, mid, low; the same formula in LaPolla 2008 fn. 2 labels them high falling / mid / low falling), stop-final syllables always high, open syllables without a tone mark unstressed; a syllable that becomes stressed by fusion 'is given a tone'. Morse 1988:128-130: register tone language, high [55] / mid [33] / low [11] plus a fourth 'neutral, non-contrastive tone' (after Morse 1962:71); 'Rawang exhibits two classes of tonally non-contrastive syllables: a) prefixal open syllables of CV-pattern in which the V is [ə]. b) closed syllables of (C)VC pattern in which the final C is a stop' -- the word 'stress' does not occur. Sarep 1996:104 (Sinwal dialect): four tonemes [55], [33], [41], [00] neutral; no stress statement. Barnard 1934: four tones, unmarked; no stress statement. tn.quote: Poko has three contrastive tonal primitives, L, M, and H. In addition, some syllables are underlyingly unspecified for tone. The three tonal primitives do not combine freely. Instead, they form the building blocks of a set of tone melodies, which are generally mirrored on mono- and disyllabic stems. In this way, Poko could be seen as an example of a word-tone system ... With the exception of /LMH/, melodies typically consist of zero to two tones, meaning that no syllable (which we could take as the tone-bearing unit/TBU) ever hosts more than two tones.

4597.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the root (the general morpheme-initial pattern), regardless of the prefixes that precede it in the polysynthetic verb or noun; monosyllabic prefixes and suffixes are unstressed, di- and polysyllabic affixes take morpheme-initial stress. 4605.dq: Toda palabra zapoteca de más de una sílaba tiene una sílaba acentuada. Las palabras aumentadas por afijos pueden tener dos o tres sílabas acentuadas, o aún cuatro. (Earl & Earl, p. 359) — corroborated by the thesis: 'en las posiciones pretónica, tónica y postónica; es decir, a inicio de palabra, la base léxica y a final de palabra' (Martínez Pérez 2019, p. 179).
4605.dloc: Gramática Zapoteca del Rincón, §0.5 'El acento y tono', pp. 359-360, read from (the PDF is font-garbled). Thesis corroboration (Martínez Pérez 2019): p. 179, Anexo 4 p. 215, p. 111, p. 124, p. 129, p. 152, pp. 37-38.
4605.prule: Stress falls 'por lo general' on the first syllable of the root. Monosyllabic prefixes and suffixes of verbs and nouns are unstressed (ri-, ru-, gu-, i-, chi-, xi-, g-, bi-, t-; -da', -u', -bi', -ru', -do', -a', -lö, -to'o, -siu'), so the word-level position shifts with affixation: penult in guba 'escoba', antepenult in yútudo' 'calabacita', fifth-from-last in ícjagacabi' 'sus cabezas', medial in rile'eda' 'veo' and chigudágubi' 'ya comió'. The same table (p. 359) also prints, without any affix segmentation, words whose stress is not on the first syllable — gubá 'sequía' (final, against guba 'escoba') and butsóa 'cicatriz' (second syllable) — so the hedge 'por lo general' is not confined to the Spanish loans; the source does not analyse these forms. When a vowel-initial root takes an aspect prefix, the prefix fuses with the root vowel and stress lands on the fused first syllable (g- + ázja + -bi' > gázjabi'; g- + úl-la + -bi' > gúl-labi'; ri- + ási + -bi' > rásibi'). Spanish loans keep Spanish stress (ximosoa', xirachua', rusumansa'-ba'). The written accent is used only when the stressed root syllable is not the penult, i.e. penult is the orthographic default, not the phonological rule. No lexical tone according to this source (contrast Martínez Pérez 2019, see the tone note).
4605.srule: Disyllabic prefixes and suffixes (íla'-, bíla'-, úlu'-, búlu'-, ta'-, -gáca, -gaqui, -tíqui'si) each carry their own stress on their first syllable in addition to the root stress, so affixed words can have two, three or even four stressed syllables (Gúla'-guítja-len-tíqui'si-gáca-bi'-ba' 'siempre jugaron con'); monosyllabic affixes are unstressed; affix stresses are not written, and the source does not rank them against the root stress. Unaffixed words have one stressed syllable.

4605.tone: The two reachable primaries disagree on tone, not on stress. Earl & Earl (p. 359): 'Aunque las palabras se distinguen por tonos en los demás dialectos del zapoteco, no hay tonos que distinguen las palabras del zapoteco del Rincón.' Martínez Pérez 2019 (p. 129, p. 135): 'hay tres tonos de nivel (alto, medio y bajo) y 6 tonos de contorno', tones carried by the tonic vowel, and the proposed orthography marks tone rather than stress because 'en Didza Xidza los tonos son más importantes que los acentos' (p. 152); the thesis (pp. 37-38) reports Schrader-Kniffki 2004 giving Yaeé only two tones (bajo, ascendente). A tone column should read 'disputed: none (Earl & Earl 2006/2011) vs 3 level + 6 contour (Martínez Pérez 2019)'. Both sources mark and use a stress position on the root, so the stress verdict is unaffected.

tn.quote: En todo el Rincón el sistema tonal Didza Xidza consta de aproximadamente 9 elementos tonales: ... hay tres tonos de nivel (alto, medio y bajo) y 6 tonos de contorno. ... De los 6 tonos de contorno, tres son ascendentes y tres son descendentes. Los ascendentes son: bajo-medio, medio-alto y bajo-alto y, los tonos de contorno descendentes son: alto-medio, medio-bajo y alto-bajo. ... Los tonos ascendente y descendente en su gran mayoría no son primitivos tonales, porque no se comportan en unidades indivisibles.
tn.translation: Throughout the Rincón the Didza Xidza tonal system consists of approximately 9 tonal elements: ... there are three level tones (high, mid and low) and 6 contour tones. ... Of the 6 contour tones, three are rising and three falling. The rising ones are low-mid, mid-high and low-high, and the falling contour tones are high-mid, mid-low and high-low. ... The rising and falling tones for the most part are not tonal primitives, because they do not behave as indivisible units.
tn.cite: Martínez Pérez, Nelson. 2019. Didza xidza / Zapoteco del Rincón: forjando su escritura a través de la descripción fonológica. Tesis de Maestría en Lingüística Aplicada, UNAM. (Earl & Earl 2006/2011 Gramática Zapoteca del Rincón §0.5 also opened: it denies lexical tone.)
tn.note: Thesis: 'approximately 9' tones, a first approximation (fn. 26): 3 levels (mid = unmarked natural register) + 6 contours, mostly level sequences; stress on root; a spectrogram. Earl & Earl deny tone. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): domain every syllable -> unstated (p.172 §6.1.2.1; p.185 cap.6); interaction with stress independent -> unstated (p.124 §3.3; Earl & Earl §0.5 denies tone).

corr.words: los tonos con que se emite cada palabra o léxico, siempre y cuando se respeten las siguientes reglas de marcación ... Además, los tonos de una sílaba o palabra pueden cambiar gramaticalmente; es decir, existen tonos léxicos y tonos gramaticales.

En esta clasificación se encuentran en el nivel fonético las vocales cortadas (checked) en sílaba tónica y con tonos de nivel: aꞋ, eꞋ, iꞋ, ɨꞋ, oꞋ y uꞋ; las vocales con laringización débil en sílaba átona (creaky voice) ... y las vocales rearticuladas (rearticulated) en sílaba tónica y con tonos de contorno

4605.cfw: Earl & Earl (2006/2011) state that stress falls on the first syllable of the root with monosyllabic prefixes and suffixes unstressed, and Martínez Pérez (2019), a native speaker describing eight Rincón communities, treats the root (base léxica) as the tonic syllable throughout, so the two first-hand descriptions agree on placement; only these two speak to stress at all (Alleman 1952 marks accents on entries but gives no rule), and their one disagreement is about whether the language also has lexical tone, not about where stress falls.

4607.prule: No placement rule stated for Ririo. Laycock's only statement is relational: Ririo 'has essentially the same stress patterns as Babatana' (said to rule out a Tongan/Rotuman-type stress-shift account of Ririo's root-final CV metathesis). The Babatana description Laycock himself relied on, Whaley 1962 (Te Reo 5: 60-62; consulted for the Babatana entry), gives no positional rule (long heavily-stressed vs short weakly-stressed vowels, length-vs-stress analysis left open). A later hedged Babatana rule exists (Palmer 2014: 159 n. 7, 'appears to involve left-aligned trochaic feet': initial stress unless a subsequent syllable has a long vowel and is heavy, reduplicants and the causative marker excluded), but Palmer says nothing about Ririo stress and Laycock's 1982 equation cannot be read as endorsing a description published 32 years later, so the equation still does not resolve to a stated Ririo stress position.
4607.srule: Not mentioned in Laycock 1982 (pp. 269-281 read in full): the only Ririo stress statement (p. 277) is that Ririo 'has essentially the same stress patterns as Babatana'; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described for Ririo (the 'penultimate syllable and every second preceding syllable' remark, p. 280, concerns Kwara'ae). 4610.dq: 同論文によれば、必須性とは語の中に「少なくとも一つの」音調上のプロミネンスを有するという性質である。この必須性と唯一性（culminativity：語は「最大ひとつの」音調上のプロミネンスを有する＝複数のプロミネンスを有さない）を同時に満たすものが、典型的なstress accent言語であるというのが同論文の提案であるが、それに従えばロンボ語は前者は満たす（あくまでも単独形でということだが）ものの後者は満たさない

4610.prule: No word-stress rule. Rombo is described as a tone language: the only clearly established toneme is /H/ (whether a marked /L/ exists is left open), syllable as TBU, surface upstepped H, H and downstepped H (≈M). Applying Hyman's (2006) criteria, the author states that Rombo satisfies obligatoriness (every isolation form carries at least one H) but not culminativity (a word may carry more than one tonal prominence), and therefore classes it as a tone language with weak accentual properties, explicitly not a stress-accent language. No positional prominence is given for any word length.
4610.srule: Not mentioned in Shinagawa 2021 (ch. 9, pp. 177-213, whole chapter read): the chapter describes tone only; its one remark on word prominence (fn. 15, p. 197) concerns tonal obligatoriness/culminativity (words may carry more than one H), not secondary stress.

4610.tone: Tone description only. Toneme inventory, p. 177 fn. 2 (verbatim): '声調素としては、明らかにそれと認められるものは/H/のみで、有標の/L/を認めるかについてはより詳細な分析が必要である。音声実現形としては、アップステップ高 [ꜛH / ꜛv́]、高 [H / v́]、ダウンステップ高 [ꜜH / ꜜv́]（ないし中 [M / v̄]）を認める。' /H/ privative (marked /L/ undecided), syllable TBU; surface ꜛH, H, ꜜH (~M). Noun stems of two syllables fall into four underlying classes -ØØ/-ØH/-HØ/-HH combined with a post-lexical H (PLH) that may spread; well-formedness constraints (sec. 2.6, tables 8-9) exclude all-L isolation forms (= obligatoriness of H) and PLH after H-initial stems. Verbs: affirmative main-clause verbs realise an H on the first or second syllable ('initial H'), absent in negatives; the syllable before negative ku is H, with optional spreading; a super-H arises when a preceding word ends in H. The stress statement is fn. 15 p. 197: Rombo meets Hyman's (2006) obligatoriness (in isolation forms only) but not culminativity, hence 'アクセント性の弱いトーン言語' (a tone language with weak accentual properties), not a stress-accent language. The 2014 sketch (sec. 1.4 p. 13) adds only: '本来すべてのチャガ系の言語は，複雑な声調（ないしアクセント）パターンを持つとされている（cf. Nurse 1977）．ただ，現在（若い世代に）話されているチャガ゠ロンボ語においては，それがかなり曖昧になっている' (all Chaga languages are said to have complex tone (or accent) patterns, much blurred in the Rombo of the young generation; lexical tone contrasts largely neutralised). The 2014 vocabulary's 'アクセント' (p. iii) refers to tone diacritics, not stress.

tn.quote: 声調素としては、明らかにそれと認められるものは/H/のみで、有標の/L/を認めるかについてはより詳細な分析が必要である。音声実現形としては、アップステップ高 [ꜛH / ꜛv́]、高 [H / v́]、ダウンステップ高 [ꜜH / ꜜv́]（ないし中[M / v̄]）を認める。 ... この言語における移動の実行単位はモーラではなく音節であることを根拠に、本稿ではこの言語の TBU を音節と解釈する。 ... つまり、音韻論的には有標の H と無標の Ø の対立のみが存在する（そして Ø は声調規則が関与しない限り [L] として実現する）privativeな体系とひとまず解釈することができる。
tn.translation: As tonemes, the only one that can clearly be recognised as such is /H/; whether a marked /L/ should be recognised requires more detailed analysis. As phonetic realisations, upstepped high [ꜛH / ꜛv́], high [H / v́] and downstepped high [ꜜH / ꜜv́] (or mid [M / v̄]) are recognised. ... On the grounds that the unit on which (tone) shift operates in this language is the syllable and not the mora, this paper interprets the TBU of this language as the syllable. ... That is, phonologically it can for the time being be interpreted as a privative system in which only the opposition between marked H and unmarked Ø exists (and Ø is realised as [L] unless a tone rule intervenes).

4612.tone: Not a tone description. Hargus & Da Conceição mention 'pitch effects caused by breathy consonants' (depressor effects) and call the penult prominence 'what sounds like penultimate stress' with undetermined phonetic correlates. Junod §57 (p. 56) distinguishes miri 'trees' from miri 'body' by 'une nuance très fine d'accentuation': rising accent on ri in 'trees', falling in 'body' -- the only tonal contrast any held source records. None of the four held sources calls Ronga a tone language; the well-known tonal status of the Tswa-Ronga group is background, not sourced here. The penult prominence is the Southern-Bantu length-plus-pitch type (Junod p. 32 §4: accented vowel generally long).

4613.prule: Count-dependent, quantity-insensitive word stress on roots: main stress is usually on the LAST syllable in words of three or more syllables ([(σ)σσσ'], e.g. ga.ra.gem', fa.ra.ge.ge'), except disyllables, which usually take stress on the first (= penultimate) syllable ([σ'σ], bha'.bha) with some variation; monosyllables are stressed. Stress is non-phonemic (non-contrastive). Four-syllable compounds show no consistent word stress (each member keeps its own stress, one primary, one secondary).
4613.srule: Only in compounds: four-syllable compounds (two member words) keep a stress on each member, one realised as the compound's main stress and the other as secondary, in at least two patterns, [[σσ'][σ`σ]] bhu.gu'.bha`.ga and [[σσ`][σ'σ]] ghe.o`.gha'.o, with other variation admitted. No secondary stress is given for simple (root) words, which carry one stress in (2-35); Suparsa 2008:283 calls non-primary nuclei 'weakly (secondarily) stressed' without any placement rule.

4616.dq: Every content word in Rukai is stressed on the last syllable, e.g. [bavá] 'wine', [tuLú] 'three', [taLagí] 'friend'. This can be accounted for by a phonological rule that assigns stress to the final syllable of a word (see 3.9).
4616.dloc: Li 1973 sec. 2.5 'Stress', p. 21; sec. 3.9 'Summary of Phonological Rules', rules (2), (5), (8), p. 63; sec. 3.5 'Echo Vowels' pp. 51-52; also sec. 2.6 p. 22; dialect identity sec. 1.3 p. 7 and p. 10. Li 1977 pp. 8, 26, 85-86; Blust 2013 pp. 173, 666-667.
4616.prule: Fixed final (Tanan dialect): primary stress on the last syllable of every content word, i.e. the last vowel of the phonological word before an optional word-final consonant or glide (rule (2) FINAL STRESS ASSIGNMENT, [+voc,-cons] --> [+stress] / __ ({[+cons] / [-voc,-cons]}) #). The rule is quantity-insensitive and counts syllables without the optional post-consonantal echo vowel, which is inserted [-stress] after stress assignment (rule (5)); consonant-final words therefore surface as e.g. [bukúl(u)] with the stressed vowel phonetically penultimate when the echo vowel is pronounced. Under emphasis or in questions the echo vowel appears and is stressed (rule (8)); the source does not say whether the rule-(2) stress is then removed. Suffixed words are stressed on their final syllable ([uŋulu-sú] 'you drink', [uŋulw-iní] 'his drinking', p. 52).

tn.quote: Tonal alignment in Budai Rukai happens at a level described by Macaulay (2021, 2023 as the IP (intonational phrase). This phrase, in all utterance types studied, ends with a final low boundary tone L% … Each IP in Budai Rukai surfaces with one pitch accent, regardless of the number of accented syllables within the IP. … It is to the final prominent syllable in the IP that the pitch accent attaches. … The pitch accent melody in declarative utterances (and words in isolation) in Budai Rukai is (L+)H*, in which the nuclear H* surfaces on the prominent syllable.
tn.cite: Macaulay, Benjamin. 2024. Speaker judgments alone cannot diagnose syllable structure. Theoretical Linguistics 50(3-4): 149-191. doi:10.1515/tl-2024-2013 (De Gruyter Brill; CC-BY open access).
tn.locator: sec. 4.4 'Intonational phonology in Budai Rukai' (article = pp. 149-191; HTML has no page numbers); TBU statements sec. 4.5, sec. 4.6, sec. 6
tn.note: Word prosody is lexical stress (penult or antepenult); pitch is analysed as intonation only: one pitch accent per phrase, (L+)H* or interrogative (L+)H*L, on the stressed syllable, then final L% or H%

4616.cfw: Li 1973, the one first-hand grammar of the Tanan dialect, states that every content word is stressed on its last syllable (bavá, tuLú, taLagí) apart from interrogatives and the monosyllabic articles, Li 1977 repeats that Tanan stress is mostly final once the echo vowels are left out of the transcription, and Blust 2013's Tanan forms (abó, comáy, cakí, ɭikoláw) fit that rule, but Li 1977 and Blust 2013 also call Rukai stress phonemic and the other dialects place it differently (Mantauran on the first syllable of the stem, Budai and Labuan mostly on the penult), so the record rests on a single fieldworker's description. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Li 1973.

4617.dq: p.4: "A word in Katiang is either monosyllabic or polysyllabic. ... Polysyllabic words are words that consist of a presyllable and a major syllable." p.5: "Phonologically, presyllable is an unstressed syllable" — the unit described is the word (sesquisyllabic word); no phrase-level prominence is discussed.
4617.dloc: Buakaw et al. 2018 pp.4-6: sec. 2.1 'Words' (p.4), sec. 2.1.2 'Polysyllabic words' (p.5), sec. 2.2 'Syllable structure' (p.6). Cross-checks: Dai & Liu 1997 pp.92-93, 96-97; Chen et al. 1986 pp.16, 18, 108.
4617.prule: Words are monosyllables (one major syllable) or sesquisyllables (presyllable + major syllable). The presyllable is unstressed and its vowel reduces to schwa; the major syllable, always word-final in a sesquisyllable, carries the stress. Position is fixed by the word template, not by weight: '01' for two-syllable words; the source assigns no stress pattern to compounds (two major syllables, or sesquisyllable + monosyllable, e.g. Ɂomtaŋ 'river', ŋɔkafaŋ 'fireplace'), so longer grids are left blank.
4617.srule: Not mentioned in Buakaw, Rattanapitak & Deepadung 2018 (sec. 2 'Katiang Phonology', pp.4-16; stress is discussed only as 'presyllable is an unstressed syllable', pp.5-6, and no stress is assigned to compounds). Weymuth 2022 (Rumai of Nam Hkam, pp.12-14, 31, 62) likewise mentions no secondary stress.

4617.idn: The cited source describes Katiang, the Palaung variety of Man Lwae village, Hsipaw (northern Shan State); its authors classify Katiang in a Katiang-Darang node sister to Rumai ('closer to Darang than other dialects of Palaung'), not as Rumai of Namhkam. The record sits under ruma1248 because Glottolog files this…
4617.exq_: No exceptions are stated. The only gap is structural: "A compound word in Katiang can be a compound of two monosyllabic words or a compound of a sesquisyllabic word and a monosyllabic word" (p.5) with no stress assignment given for compounds.
4617.tone: Katiang (Buakaw et al. 2018): the word 'tone' does not occur anywhere in the 16-page phonology; the description is non-tonal. The varieties actually named Rumai in Yunnan are tonal: Dai & Liu 1997 p.92 "Guangka is a subdialect of the Rumai dialect of De'ang... Guangka has three tones; almost every syllable has a fixed tone, and there are many tonal minimal pairs"; p.93 "In addition to the above three tones, Guangka has a 31 tone. This tone only appears in the first (weakened) syllable of polysyllabic words, and in borrowings from Chinese"; p.96 "Guangka still has a few words without fixed tone"; p.97 "Chayeqing has high level and high falling tones" (Chayeqing = Rumai subdialect) while "Yungqian does not have tones" (Bulei) and "Xiaochanggou also lacks tones" (Liang). Chen et al. 1986 p.108 (Rumai dialect sketch): 汝买话不仅有元音长短的区别，而且还有声调的区分... 只分高平调〔55〕和全降调〔51〕两个调 (two tones); p.16 (Bulei base variety): 德昂语虽然没有声调（字调）(no lexical tone). Neither Chinese-language source uses the word 重音 (stress) for the major syllable; both describe the presyllable vowel as 轻读/弱化 ('read lightly, weakened'): p.18 一般音节中的元音是固定的，清晰的，不是轻读的，而前加音节中的元音，始终是以轻读、弱化形式出现，含糊不清，很不稳定 (checked on the scan, and previously by the compilers on).

4617.cfw: Buakaw, Rattanapitak and Deepadung 2018 describe the Katiang presyllable as unstressed with the main syllable carrying the stress, Weymuth 2022 independently reports an iambic structure for Rumai of Nam Hkam in which prefixes are never stressed and the second word of a compound is stressed, and Chen, Wang and Lai 1986 and Dai and Liu 1997 describe the same weakened presyllables in the Chinese De'ang and Guangka Rumai varieties, with no source disagreeing.
